title: Ask about the light, not the caste
hookLine: recognize the light in everyone and do not ask their caste (Asa, ang 349)

lines: WHERE ARE YOU FROM? WHAT DO YOU DO?
cards: Where are you from? What do you do? Where did you go to school?
What's your last name? Those questions can be friendly. They can also be a way of sorting, placing someone on a ladder before you know them at all.

In Guru Nanak's world, the big sorting question was caste, the group you were born into, which could decide whom you ate with and whom you married. Guru Nanak had a one-line answer: ask about the light.

teach.b: On Ang 349, in Rag Asa, Guru Nanak sings: jaanahu jot na poochhahu jaatee aagai jaat na he. Recognize the light, don't ask about caste; in the world beyond, there is no caste.
Jot is light, the divine light Sikhs believe shines in every person. Jaat is caste, birth-group.

And the verbs are the point: jaanahu, know, recognize; na poochhahu, don't even ask. Guru Nanak isn't only saying caste doesn't matter to God. He's saying don't make it the first question you put to a human being.
The Gurus didn't leave this as a nice sentence. They built it into furniture and food.

teach.h: ONE ROW, ONE MEAL: THE PANGAT.
teach.b: In the langar, the free kitchen, everyone sits on the floor in the same rows, the pangat, and eats the same meal, whoever they are.
Tradition tells that Guru Amar Das asked visitors, even the Mughal emperor Akbar, to eat in the langar before meeting him.
Later, tradition says, when Guru Gobind Singh created the Khalsa, the five who first stepped forward came from different castes and regions, and they drank amrit from one bowl.
Caste didn't vanish from Punjabi life, Sikh life included, and the line still challenges the communities that sing it. But the rule on paper is clear, and it's short.
Before you ask what someone's label is, see what's shining in them.

how: In the gurdwara langar, people of any background sit together in rows (pangat) on the floor and eat the same free meal; Sikh teaching rejects caste distinctions, though caste still shapes parts of community life.

o: the caste or group you are born into
the divine light shining in every person
a lamp lit before the Guru Granth Sahib

games.q: inside Guru Nanak's line — tap the pairs.

s: Guru Nanak's line says caste only matters in the next life
it says recognize the light and don't ask about caste; beyond this world there is no caste.
tradition says the first five of the Khalsa came from different castes
and they drank amrit from one bowl.
in the langar, important guests get separate tables
everyone sits in the same rows, the pangat, and eats the same meal.

games.q: tradition says the Mughal emperor Akbar came to see Guru Amar Das. what did the Guru ask first?
o: that Akbar be seated on a throne above everyone.
that he eat in the langar, sitting with everyone else.
that he state his caste and rank.
games.why: tradition says the emperor sat in the pangat and ate the same meal before meeting the Guru.

practice: Bring to mind someone you usually file under a label, the new hire, the neighbor, the person at the counter, the relative you've decided about, and set the label down, the way you'd set down a bag.
Look at them again in your mind: a face, a life, a light. Breathe in and silently say, see the light; breathe out, and stay here a while.

wordCard.voice: Jot, light, the divine light in every person. Guru Nanak's line in Asa: recognize it, and don't ask their caste.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: jot, light; jaanahu jot na poochhahu jaatee, recognize the light, don't ask the caste.

carryVoice: Your line: see the light. One row, one meal, one bowl. See you next time.
